summary: Reports on tests of what happens to common Internet applications when service providers add a second layer of NAT (carrier-grade NAT, as in NAT444) while transitioning to IPv6. It identifies where the extra translation breaks or degrades applications, and was updated to cover Dual-Stack Lite as well.

eli5.summary: When your message passes through two translators instead of one, some things get lost in translation. This lists which things go wrong.

subtitle: Lab results showing which everyday Internet applications break or slow down behind a second, carrier-grade layer of NAT.

tldr.problem: As IPv4 addresses ran out, service providers considered NAT444 and Dual-Stack Lite, which put many customers behind one IPv4 address, and it was unclear how that would affect popular applications.
tldr.mechanism: CableLabs, Time Warner Cable and Rogers Communications ran lab tests in 2010 and 2011 of many applications across several network topologies, with and without a carrier-grade NAT (CGN) in the path.
tldr.outcome: Web browsing and email worked, but peer-to-peer applications, direct SIP calls and BitTorrent seeding failed, some transfers and streams slowed down, and address sharing caused geolocation, abuse-tracing and anti-spoofing problems.

today: RFC 7021 is an Informational document from the Independent Submission stream and is not marked obsoleted or updated. It reports results from tests run in 2010 and 2011, so its findings describe that equipment and those applications.

sections.title: Why CGN Was Tested
sections.content:
The RFC says IANA, APNIC and RIPE NCC exhausted their IPv4 address space in 2011-2012, and that the move to IPv6 would not finish before IPv4 ran out. NAT444 and Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite, RFC 6333) are transition mechanisms that let a provider multiplex customers behind a single IPv4 address. Both give basic IPv4 connectivity, but they affect advanced applications.

Testing ran in two rounds. From July through August 2010, CableLabs, Time Warner Cable and Rogers Communications tested NAT444. From June through October 2011, CableLabs tested NAT444 and DS-Lite, working with vendors including A10, Alcatel-Lucent and Juniper to optimize the applications that did badly earlier. The document was updated to add the DS-Lite results.
sections.eli5: The world ran out of old-style addresses, so providers made many homes share one. This asks what breaks when homes share.

sections.title: How the Tests Were Run
sections.content:
Four test cases were used: one client in one home network; two clients in one home network; two clients in two home networks on the same provider; and two clients in two home networks on two providers. The lab emulated provider networks with a CGN behind cable modem termination systems, cable modems, home routers and clients such as laptops, gaming consoles, tablets, smartphones and Blu-ray players.

Applications included video streaming (Netflix, YouTube), peer-to-peer file sharing, Xbox gaming, FTP, SIP calls, Skype, social networking and web conferencing. Metrics were throughput, latency and jitter, compared with the CGN in place, removed, and reconfigured. Latency and jitter differed only slightly, but the testers did not do load testing and limited measurements to single sessions. Some NAT444 tests used RFC 1918 private space between the CGN and the home router and others used public space; results matched except for 6to4.
sections.eli5: They built a pretend neighborhood in a lab with many kinds of gadgets and tried the same things with and without the shared address.

sections.title: What Broke and What Slowed Down
sections.content:
Basic services such as email and web browsing worked as expected. Impacts to NAT444 and DS-Lite were similar except where noted.

Dropped services: peer-to-peer Xbox gaming and direct peer-to-peer SIP calls with the PJSIP client failed. Some applications never send outgoing traffic first, so they never open an incoming port, and others insist on one fixed port that only one subscriber can hold. Direct BitTorrent and uTorrent seeding failed, although the session usually succeeded by being redirected to a proxy server. Raising the STUN timeout to 4 minutes helped uTorrent. FTP to servers inside the home failed, and multicast was not forwarded through the CGN. In 2010, 6to4 and Teredo also failed or degraded badly.

Performance: large transfers and multiple video sessions from one client were slower. With DS-Lite, one example showed 120 kbps for one PC against 250 kbps for another behind the same router, and the authors suspect the MTU. On one popular older router, a first stream stopped for 8 s when a second started. Video buffering was longer but then smooth.

Since 2010 things improved through content provider updates, application updates (STUN, proxies) and better CGNs. Port reservations helped SIP, but a reservation on port 5060 can serve only one user.
sections.eli5: Games and calls that need two people to find each other directly got confused, because both seemed to live at the same address. Watching videos mostly worked but took longer to start.

sections.title: Wider Side Effects of Sharing Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC lists problems beyond application tests. Geolocation suffers because translation zones cross geographic boundaries and the outside address no longer maps to a place. Lawful intercept and abuse response become harder because the source address alone does not identify a customer, so logging source port and timestamp is needed (see RFC 6269). Anti-spoofing and DDoS protection may be triggered by traffic from one shared address, and anti-spam rules that limit connections per address can wrongly block many users.

Mitigation was not the focus, but the RFC tabulates ideas: a proxy server or the Port Control Protocol (RFC 6887) for peer-to-peer and gaming, placing the CGN near the network edge with regional address and port assignment for geolocation, and deterministic or bulk port logging for lawful intercept.
sections.eli5: When a whole street shares one mailbox number, it is hard for anyone to tell which house a letter came from, or to know where the street even is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC points to RFC 6264 and RFC 6269. It adds that a CGN shares one IPv4 address among many subscribers, which may make it an attractive denial-of-service target, and that abuse attribution needs content providers to log the address, source port and time so they can be matched with provider logs. If a CGN address lands on a blacklist, or a server limits connections per address, legitimate users can suffer.
sections.eli5: If one address is shared by many people, one troublemaker can get everyone on it blocked.
